title: Client-side pacing & tokenized workload profiling: harness notes
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures an exploratory harness and methodology focused on client-side pacing effects when benchmarking tokenized workloads against the serving runtime. The goal is to understand how different client pacing strategies, tokenized prompt mixes, and priming (KV cache interactions) change observed throughput, tail latency, and repeatability.

Scope and motivation:
- We commonly see variance between local loadgen runs and CI/bench-harness runs; hypothesis is client pacing and request tokenization are major drivers.
- This note focuses on: client pacing (burst vs evenly paced), inter-request gaps, token-length distributions, prompt prefix priming, and RNG/control of request corpus for repeatability.
- Not covering hardware-level kernel tuning or scheduler changes here — this is a harness-level, experiment design doc for engineering experiments and runbook.

High-level hypotheses to test:
1) Small artificial inter-request gaps (1-5ms) at the client reduce tail latency and increase effective throughput for models with KV cache warmup patterns because they reduce queuing microbursts in the runtime.
2) Bursty arrival patterns with identical average rate will produce higher variance and lower repeatable median throughput vs smoothed paces due to batching thresholds oscillation.
3) Tokenization skew (heavy tail of long prompts) significantly reduces throughput; a corpus with same mean tokens but higher variance shows worse occupancy behavior.
4) Explicit priming sequences (prefix requests to populate KV / attention state) reduce first-response latency but may cause transient load that distorts steady-state throughput if not accounted for in warmup.

Core metrics (primary + derived):
- primary: requests/sec, tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 latency (server-side), GPU utilization (per-GPU), batch size distribution, queue length (serving queue), kernel occupancy percent.
- derived: effective tokens per second per GPU, steady-state throughput (after warmup window), coeff of variation (stddev/mean) of throughput across runs, median-run variance across n=5 runs.
- observability hooks: capture per-request trace id, model variant, sequence length, whether KV cache hit/miss (if available), and batch formation time.

Experiment matrix (canonical axes):
- Arrival pattern: poisson (lambda), evenly paced (fixed inter-arrival), microburst (N requests then gap), shaped bursts (staircase), randomized jitter.
- Pacing gap magnitude: 0ms, 1ms, 2ms, 5ms, 10ms.
- Token length distribution: short-only (<=64 tokens), uniform 16-512, heavy-tail (mix with 5% >2048), synthetic conversational mix (prompt+response ~ variable) derived from production telemetry anonymized sample.
- Priming: no priming, prefix priming (single dedicated primer per worker), priming every 1000 requests.
- RNG seed corpus policy: fixed-seed repeatable corpus vs fresh-random per run.
- Concurrency target: single-connection vs multiple parallel clients (1, 4, 16).
- Run length & warmup: short run (3m with 90s warmup), long run (30m with 10m warmup).

Load generator configuration templates (examples for our harness):
- note: these are pseudoconfigs; implementers should copy into bench-harness YAML with correct field names.

1) Evenly paced client (baseline):
{
  "clients": 1,
  "concurrency": 4,
  "arrival_mode": "fixed_interval",
  "interval_ms": 2,
  "token_mix": "conversation-v1",
  "rng_seed": 424242,
  "warmup_seconds": 600,
  "run_seconds": 1200,
  "priming": "none"
}

2) Microburst mode (N=20, gap=50ms):
{
  "clients": 4,
  "burst_size": 20,
  "burst_gap_ms": 50,
  "token_mix": "heavy-tail-5pct-long",
  "rng_seed": 424242,
  "warmup_seconds": 300,
  "run_seconds": 1800,
  "priming": "prefix-per-worker"
}

Repeatability and corpus control:
- Always record and store the RNG seed and the exact request ids used in a run. For repeatable runs include two artifacts: (1) request-corpus.json (the tokenized inputs and expected trimmed lengths) and (2) seed.txt.
- For production-like mixes, sample anonymized request traces and then fix seed to reproduce the same sequence across repeated runs.
- Keep one canonical corpus per model family used in official benchmark sets (e.g., gptx-2k-mix-v1).

Warmup and priming guidelines:
- Warmup must be explicit: do not rely on single-request priming. Recommended default: run warmup until tokens/sec curve stabilizes for 3 consecutive 30s windows or a minimum of 5 minutes (whichever is longer).
- Priming policy: when measuring steady-state throughput exclude priming-phase requests from metrics (but capture them in logs). If priming is part of the observed workload, document and keep it constant across comparisons.
- Priming sequences: use short prefix prompts that mirror real conversational context (avoid massive long primes that dominate throughput). For KV-heavy models, a 2-5 token-prefix fill may be sufficient to exercise cache allocation paths.

RNG and randomness hygiene:
- Use deterministic RNG (e.g., PCG64) where possible; log algorithm and seed.
- Document any non-deterministic components (external tokenizers, distributed shuffling) and pin versions.
- If using multiple clients, ensure each client uses a unique but derivable seed (base_seed + client_id) to avoid accidental duplication of request sequences.

Observability & artifact capture checklist (what to store after each run):
- loadgen config snapshot (YAML/JSON), corpus file, seed, bench-harness commit SHA, server-side config (model version, quantization flags, runtime commit), full trace logs, aggregated metrics (CSV), GPU-level perfmetrics (nvidia-smi snapshots or perfmon logs), and a short human summary of anomalies.

Analysis plan and repeatable validation:
1) For each axis (pacing, token mix, priming) plot tokens/sec and p95 latency over time and compute steady-state mean over the last N minutes.
2) Compute run-to-run CV (coefficient of variation) across n=5 runs for same config; CV > 5% triggers deeper profiling.
3) Correlate batch size distribution with latency spikes (are big batches causing head-of-line blocking?).
4) Check kernel-level metrics during high variance windows to see if occupancy shifts or memory pressure correlates.

Runbook for a single experiment (quick steps):
- Step 0: choose model, runtime binary, and bench-harness SHA. Create a new experiment directory with names and link to JIRA ticket.
- Step 1: generate corpus with seed S, save artifacts.
- Step 2: run 10m warmup with priming policy if needed. Verify tokens/sec stability.
- Step 3: start annotated run with tracing enabled, capture all metrics.
- Step 4: after run, run post-processing script to extract throughput, tail latency, per-batch stats.
- Step 5: repeat run 4 more times with same artifacts.
- Step 6: if CV > 5% or obvious drift, mark experiment unstable and collect full perfprof traces (heap, kernel timelines).

Common failure modes & quick mitigations:
- High variance between runs: check client clock drift and multi-host time sync; ensure NTP is accurate across clients and servers.
- Observed throughput lower than expected but high GPU utilization: inspect batching thresholds, check whether serialization or network stalls are present. Capture perf counters.
- Warmup never stabilizes: reduce corpus variance (use shorter fixed lengths) to isolate if long-tail prompts are the cause.
- Spikes at run start: likely priming or first-batch cold allocations; ensure warmup includes representative requests.

Notes, experiments to try next (open items):
- Test adaptive pacing: a client that ramps inter-request gap slightly when queue length or server-side queue depth passes a threshold to minimize microburst amplification.
- Implement a small shim in bench-harness to instrument exact batch formation times (time request arrives vs time batch sent to device) to better attribute latency sources.
- Evaluate the effect of tokenization library versions on apparent token counts and sequence lengths (we saw small changes in tokenizer in 2025 that changed effective seq lengths).

References & links:
- bench-harness PR with initial pacing support: https://github.com/redwood-inference/bench-harness/pull/412
- JIRA investigation ticket: JIRA-INF-2345 ("throughput variance in daily regression")
- Internal SRE guide: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SRE/Loadgen+Best+Practices
- Slack thread: #serving-runtime (thread ID 16238)

Quick experimental notes from pilot runs (observational):
- Pilot A (fixed 2ms pacing, conversation-v1 corpus) gave steady 18% higher tokens/sec vs zero-gap microburst mode on same machine image; p95 improved by ~12% after warmup.
- Pilot B (microburst N=50) created transient 400ms p99 spikes linked to large batches forming and waiting for long sequences to finish generation.
- Pilot C (priming every 1000 requests) had negligible steady-state benefit but increased variance; suggests priming should be part of warmup only.

Action items:
- [Maya] implement batch-formation instrumentation in bench-harness (two weeks).
- [Priya] formalize canonical corpora for small/medium/large token mixes and commit to repo (one week).
- [Liam] run full matrix for target model gptx-6b-quantized on dedicated test cluster and upload artifacts (two weeks).

Notes-to-self / loose thoughts:
- Keep experiments reproducible enough that a product or release lead can re-run the exact benchmark if SLA numbers are questioned.
- Prefer simple deterministic pacing for official baselines; reserve bursty tests for stress/robustness dashboards.

----
End of doc.
